job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior test engineer at a payments company in Cork, so I spend my day writing automated checks that make sure the app doesn't lose people's money. I stand up at ten for the team meeting, write tests until lunch, and then chase a developer called Declan about a bug that keeps coming back. I studied software engineering and passed, with no placement, because the placement spots all went to the top of the class. I live in a house share with three others, and my girlfriend Siobhan, a nurse, works nights, so we mostly meet at weekends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How's the job treating you, and what do you do for fun?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's good. The pay is better than I expected, and my parents (Dad's a plumber, Mum manages a shop) told me they'd put in towards a deposit when I'm ready. For fun I play five-a-side on Wednesdays and go to Cork City matches with my dad. The part I like is finding the bug nobody else spotted. The part I don't is how much of my work is just repeating tests, which I'm sure could be done by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and no more. At work I'd tell Declan it helps me write a first draft of a test, but I still rewrite half. To the lads at football I'd say all the doom talk was a bit much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. My job has a lot of repetition, and a bit of help is welcome. I'd keep learning the tools when the team does, because I'm not the first to try things, but I'm not the last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, take a couple of testing certificates, and put 700 euros a month into the deposit fund. I'd talk to Siobhan about renting a flat together in two years. I'd keep my Wednesday football and my dad's match days, because they keep me level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd enjoy my twenties and just get on. It would feel like a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What would that look like in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tool on a Tuesday to make tests faster and then put the time into the harder bugs. It would give me more room to be useful. Ideally the firm would see that and not just cut a tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What in your life would still weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, honestly. A flat in Cork with my girlfriend Siobhan would be nearly half my pay. Her night shifts are hard on her, and she'd like to cut hours, which the rent would not allow. That's the pressure I'd carry.

say: It's a decent **tool** and no more, and the doom talk was a bit much.
I'd tell Declan (a developer at my firm) it helps with first drafts, but I **rewrite** half.
think: My job has a lot of **repetition**, so a bit of help is welcome.
I'm not the first to try things, but I'm not the **last**.
do: Take a couple of **testing certificates** and put 700 euros a month into the deposit fund.
Talk to **Siobhan** about renting a flat together in two years.
Keep my Wednesday **football** and my dad's match days.
S0.quote: A flat in Cork with my girlfriend Siobhan would be nearly half my pay.
fieldNote: His pressure is **rent**, not AI, and it touches his girlfriend's hours.
He uses AI to free time for **harder** bugs, a steady adopter's pattern.
Family help gives a calm base, but not freedom.

steps.text: Take two software testing certificates this year
Put 700 euros a month into the deposit fund
Use AI to draft tests and spend the time on hard bugs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change, and companies should be honest about it. At work I'd say let's use the tools well so we're not the ones replaced. I'd tell the lads that testers are the canary in the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think testing is one of the first things to go. Writing and running checks is a pure thinking task, and a machine can do it all day without a break. If the firm cuts a tester, it's me or Brigid, the other junior, and I'm the one with the pass degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Declan to put me on the exploratory testing side, because that's human judgement, not just scripts. I'd learn the AI testing tools once my team adopts them in the next few months. I'd also build up my savings to about 6,000 euros over the year, so I'm safe if I'm cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a long way from panic, but I can feel the pressure on my job. And I'm not at all sure the firm would warn us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your test engineer role look like if checks write themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the person who reviews what the AI tests, which is a smaller job than writing them. The team might go from four testers to two. I'd be fighting to be one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Siobhan react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Siobhan would say I'm worrying early. She's a nurse, so she's not worried about her job, and I'd say that's a relief for us. But she'd also say if I need to change, we'll manage, which is lovely, and not nothing.

say: It's a real change, and companies should be **honest** about it.
I'd tell the lads that testers are the **canary** in the mine.
think: Writing and running checks is a pure **thinking** task, and a machine can do it all day.
If the firm cuts a tester, it's me or **Brigid**, the other junior.
do: Ask Declan to put me on **exploratory** testing, where human judgement matters.
Learn the AI testing **tools** once my team adopts them.
Build savings to about **6,000 euros** over the year.
feel: **Anxious**, a long way from panic, but I feel pressure on my job.

fieldNote: He names the **exact** task at risk and the colleague who competes with him.

A nurse partner gives the household a safer earner.

steps.text: Ask Declan to move me onto exploratory testing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should get a grip, and we need to know what the plan is. I'd also say firms should give long notice. I'm not a protester, but I'd back anything that gave ordinary people time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels like two years to find a new life. The testing job's gone, and my pass degree isn't going to open doors if every graduate is chasing the same ones. Robots come about 2031, so hands-on trades could last longer than my desk does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard, pay off nothing early and keep cash. I'd talk to my dad about plumbing, because he knows people and the trade lasts longer. I'd also ask a heating-engineer friend about a conversion course. I'd tell my girlfriend that we're not renting a flat for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake at night. I think I'm in the group that loses the job and I don't see a quick route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you rely on when the testing jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, mostly, and Siobhan. Dad would say come and train with me, and he'd mean it. I'd feel a bit embarrassed saying yes, with a degree. But I'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you split what you'd say publicly from what you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd keep it light, because I don't want to scare people. At home I'd be honest. I told my girlfriend Siobhan once that I'd be fine, and she said, you say that when you're not fine. She's right.

say: The government should get a grip, and firms should give **long notice**.
I'd back anything that gave ordinary people **time**.
think: It feels like two years to find a **new life**, because the testing job's gone.
A pass degree won't open doors if every graduate chases the **same** ones.
do: Talk to my dad about **plumbing** and ask a heating engineer about a course.
Tell my girlfriend we're not renting a **flat** for now.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake, sure I'm in the group that loses the job.
S2.quote: I told my girlfriend Siobhan once that I'd be fine, and she said, you say that when you're not fine.
fieldNote: His **say** and **think** differ clearly, and he knows it.
The trades route via his father is a real, embarrassing but accepted fallback.
His mood is the highest of the nine because testing is directly in the line of fire.

steps.text: Cut spending to the basics and keep cash
Train with my dad on plumbing jobs on Saturdays
Ask a heating engineer about a conversion course
Tell Siobhan the flat plan is on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so use it. I'd say it to my team: let's pick up the tools, and let's ask the firm what it plans. I'd say it to the lads: stop joking and get a trade skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel a bit better. Five years means I could do a part-time degree or a trade certificate and still be in work at 27. The worry is that the ladder for juniors thins before then, and I'm the one stuck on the bottom rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move from testing into something that needs people, such as business analysis, within two years. I'd take an evening course, about 1,500 euros, and use my savings for it. I'd also learn the AI testing tools properly this time, not just dabble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a handle on it. Five years means I'm not sitting waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for the choices you make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a proper plan: course, move internally, maybe move cities. Two years was just survival. The difference is that I can think about Siobhan and a flat rather than only my own skin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Brigid, the other junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Brigid to get into analysis too, and to not wait for the firm to tell us. She's good, but she assumes someone will look after her. I'd share what I learned, because it's no good being the only one who lands.

I'd tell the lads to stop joking and get a **trade skill**.

steps.text: Apply for a business analyst move inside the firm
Take an evening business analysis course for 1,500 euros
Learn the AI testing tools in depth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case, so let's not waste it. I'd say to my team that we should adopt the tools slowly and carefully. I'd say to the lads that the fear is a bit much and the plan is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm mostly fine. At 32 I'd be in my thirties with a flat, maybe a child, maybe a different job. I'd feel that I had time, which is more than two years allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a flat with Siobhan in three years, using my deposit fund and my parents' help. I'd keep my testing job but move into team lead or analysis. I'd also try a part-time degree in data or product management, since those might hold their value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly fine. It's a long time, and I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in how you plan for a flat and family with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd go for the flat sooner, and I'd think about a child at 28 or 29. I wouldn't wait for AGI to be settled. If I did, I'd never do any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good public retraining scheme, so that I'm not paying for it all. And honest information from the government, in plain words, on what's coming and when. I'd also like my firm to give people time to shift between roles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Testing is exactly the work a machine does, and two years isn't enough to build a new life. What would help is plain information from government, a retraining scheme that doesn't leave me in debt and time from my firm to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more worried than I come across. I joke a lot, and people think that means I'm fine.

headlineQuote: I joke a lot, and people think that means I'm fine.
portrait: Pedro is **22**, a junior test engineer at a Cork payments firm, with a pass degree in software engineering and no placement.
He uses AI **now and then**, adopts tools once colleagues do, and has parents ready to help with a deposit.
He is a pragmatic centrist whose girlfriend Siobhan, a nurse, gives the household a **safer** earner.
Testing is directly exposed, so his mood runs from calm to **alarmed** at the 2-year picture, then eases with time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because testing is exactly the work a **machine** does.
whatWouldHelp: **Plain** information from government, retraining without debt and time from his firm to move roles.
